contentHtml:
Two colleagues, both 45, take the stairs at the office. One reaches the fourth floor without a pause; the other stops at the second landing to catch his breath. Their birth certificates say they are the same age. Their bodies may disagree by a decade.

That gap is what scientists call biological age. It may be the most useful health number most Indians have never heard of.

Living longer, but not living well

India has made remarkable gains in longevity. A child born in 1951 could expect to live about 37 years; today, life expectancy at birth is around 72.5 years. Yet the World Health Organization puts India’s healthy life expectancy at roughly 58 years. On average, that leaves about 14 years lived with illness or disability.

This is the real challenge of longevity: not adding years to life, but adding life to years. Medicine calls it healthspan, and on that measure India has work to do.

The International Diabetes Federation’s 2025 Diabetes Atlas estimates that about 90 million Indian adults were living with diabetes in 2024. Of them, 43 per cent, roughly 38.6 million people, did not know it. The ICMR-INDIAB study, India’s largest metabolic survey, counted another 136 million people with prediabetes. These conditions rarely announce themselves. By the time symptoms appear, years of silent damage have often been done.

What biological age actually measures

Chronological age counts birthdays. Biological age reflects how your cells, organs and systems are actually functioning. Genes play a part, but sleep, stress, diet, physical activity and even air quality push it up or down.

Scientists estimate it using biomarkers, measurable signals in the body that work much like the warning lights on a car’s dashboard. One of the most widely studied methods, PhenoAge, was developed by researchers at Yale in 2018. It combines nine routine blood markers with a person’s age. In the original research, every additional year of PhenoAge was linked to a 9 per cent higher risk of death from any cause, and a 20 per cent higher risk of death from diabetes.

More recent work shows how wide the gap can be. A 2025 analysis of over three lakh participants in the UK Biobank found that, based on blood markers alone, biological age ranged from 20 years younger to 20 years older than actual age.

The answers are already in routine reports

What makes this science relevant for India is that it does not depend on exotic tests. Most PhenoAge markers sit inside investigations millions of Indians already take. A complete blood count captures white blood cells, lymphocytes and red cell measures. Liver and kidney function tests cover albumin, alkaline phosphatase and creatinine. Fasting glucose or HbA1c tracks blood sugar, and a high-sensitivity CRP test reveals hidden inflammation.

Add cholesterol, thyroid, vitamin B12 and vitamin D, and a far fuller picture emerges. Vitamin D alone tells a striking story. Despite abundant sunshine, a 2025 report by ICRIER and the ANVKA Foundation found one in five Indians deficient, with rates close to 39 per cent in eastern India.

The problem is not access to data. It is what happens to it. Too often a report is filed away because every value sits within the “normal range”, even when the numbers have been drifting in the wrong direction for years.

The clock can be turned back

The most hopeful finding in longevity science is that biological age is not fixed. In a 2021 randomised trial, 43 men aged 50 to 72 followed an eight-week programme: a plant-rich diet, at least seven hours of sleep, 30 minutes of exercise five days a week, and breathing exercises for stress. At the end, their biological age measured 3.23 years younger than the control group’s. The study was small, but the direction was clear. Everyday habits move the needle.

Global interest is surging. The biological age testing market is projected to grow from about $1.15 billion in 2025 to $1.33 billion in 2026, and longevity clinics abroad charge premium prices for advanced panels. For most Indians, though, the starting point is far simpler and far more affordable.

From reports to healthspan

If India is serious about healthy ageing, it must make three shifts.

First, preventive testing must become an annual habit, not a reaction to symptoms. A yearly panel covering blood count, liver, kidney, sugar, lipids, inflammation and key vitamins can flag risks years before they turn into disease.

Second, people must track trends, not snapshots. A single report is a photograph; three reports a year apart tell a story. Digital health records now make it possible to spot a value slowly drifting long before it crosses a red line.

Third, the diagnostics industry must move from delivering reports to delivering understanding. Doorstep sample collection, transparent pricing and plain-language interpretation, increasingly powered by AI, can turn a page of numbers into clear next steps. And when values are out of range, that understanding must lead people to a qualified doctor, not an internet search.

The number you can change

Return to the two colleagues on the staircase. Neither can change the year he was born. Both can change the age their bodies are living at.

Longevity does not begin in an expensive clinic. It begins with a routine blood test, read carefully and acted upon. In a country where millions have undiagnosed conditions, this may be the most powerful health habit of all.
